notes: \cpara{Names the fallacy, the author's own term from the linked chapter, and gives the example of a journalist who recalls the \textsc{Terminator} films in a report on AI as if they were a historical case.}
\cpara{States the thesis: the inverse error is being moved too little by history, which did happen.}
\cpara{Explains both errors by the ancestral environment, in the form of a question (``Is it any wonder''). No evidence is given for either half of the story.}
\cpara{Describes the inverse error: history processed like a novel, called true but not felt.}

\cpara{Returns to the author's episode: vitalism's rise and fall happened to real people. The claim that living through past revolutions would have prevented another mysterious answer is hedged here (``I probably would not''). Lord Kelvin, a vitalist who did live through one, is discussed in the notes on ``Failing to Learn from History.''}
\cpara{The remedy: think as if everything in the history books had happened to you, and immerse yourself in eras known only from print.}

\cpara{Argues by a question: ``Is there so much difference'' between seeing an event and reading about it, since both reach us by causal chains? The post's own footnote gives one difference, that history books over-represent rulers. The paragraph does not take it up.}
\cpara{Calls the lack of such memories a ``false amnesia'' and resolves to make all of history available, not only one's own era.}
\cpara{Illustrates: the author now ``remembers'' the rise and fall of Rome, and the modern world seems more fragile.}
\cpara{Draws the lesson: mistakes repeat because we do not remember making them.}
\cpara{A joke: you do not remember your biases killing you because death follows; ``I remember; I wasn't there.''}

\cpara{The exercise asks the reader to remember history in the first person, with particulars (the tribe, the mushrooms) that the reader must imagine. The opening paragraph said that vividly imagined cases are how fiction comes to be treated as evidence. The post does not say how to keep the imagined parts of history from doing the same; its one safeguard is the footnote on reweighting.}
\cpara{The method's one caveat: history books over-represent rulers, so one should remember ``a thousand peasants for every ruler.''}
